claims.text: A designed mixture approach is a specialized design-of-experiments method for multicomponent systems.
Systematically varying Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr content will quantify each element's individual effect on mechanical properties.
The composition study will reveal an optimal compositional window with improved strength-ductility synergy.
The initial material is an as-cast HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy with near-equiatomic proportions.
Vacuum arc melting followed by homogenization heat treatment can provide comparative metallurgical states before mechanical testing.
Changing the relative elemental percentages can alter phase constitution.
Changing the relative elemental percentages can alter grain morphology and lattice distortion.
Element-specific compositional variations alter local bonding.
Element-specific compositional variations alter lattice distortion.
Changes in local bonding and lattice distortion affect dislocation movement and strengthening mechanisms.
Some nonequiatomic HfNbTaTiZr compositions will exhibit greater tensile strength than the equiatomic baseline.
Some nonequiatomic HfNbTaTiZr compositions will exhibit greater ductility than the equiatomic baseline.
The fully equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy has established yield-strength and tensile-property values under comparable processing.
Excessive deviation from near-equiatomic ratios may induce brittle phases.
Excessive deviation from near-equiatomic ratios may induce segregation.
Brittle phases or segregation would limit the alloy's overall mechanical performance.
The exact optimal composition remains unverified without targeted experimental data.
